prompt: On a logic analyser, you time a single three-byte Note On arriving over DIN MIDI, from the start of its first start bit to the end of its last stop bit. It takes just under 1 ms. What does this tell you?

options.text: The link is running at the wrong baud rate, because three bytes should take about 0.1 ms
options.explanation: That expectation assumes a link roughly ten times faster. At 31,250 bit/s, three framed bytes really do take close to a millisecond.

options.text: Nothing is wrong: each byte occupies ten bit-times, so three back-to-back bytes take just under 1 ms
options.explanation: Correct. Thirty framed bits at 31,250 bit/s is about 0.96 ms. This is normal DIN MIDI wire time.

options.text: The sender is inserting gaps, because 24 data bits should take only about 0.77 ms
options.explanation: This forgets the start and stop bits. Each byte is framed as 10 bits on the wire, not 8.

options.text: The bytes are arriving in parallel, so the whole message should take a single bit-time
options.explanation: MIDI is serial: one bit at a time on one current loop. A single bit-time (32 µs) is only one thirtieth of the message.

workedExample:
1. DIN MIDI runs at 31,250 bits per second (MIDI electrical specification).
2. Each byte is framed with a start bit and a stop bit around its 8 data bits, so it costs 10 bit-times: 320 µs.
3. Three bytes back to back are 30 bit-times, a little under 1 ms.
4. So a measurement just under 1 ms means the link is behaving exactly as specified. Expecting less usually means forgetting the framing bits or assuming a faster transport.

The practical consequence: DIN MIDI carries only about 1,000 three-byte messages per second, which is why dense controller data can delay notes.

prompt: A sequencer sends a 10-note chord over DIN MIDI as ten complete three-byte Note On messages, all scheduled for the same instant. Each message takes about 0.96 ms on the wire. Roughly how far apart in time do the first and last notes start?

options.text: 0 ms: messages scheduled together arrive together
options.explanation: DIN MIDI is a single serial line; only one byte can be on the wire at a time.
That is the time for just one byte, not ten messages.
Correct. The first note can start once its message completes; each later note waits for one more message, so the last starts nine message-times later: about 8.6 ms.
That is ten times too long: it treats each message as taking about 9.6 ms, which is the time for all ten together.

workedExample:
1. DIN MIDI is a single serial line, so the ten messages go out one after another.
2. The first note can start when its own message has fully arrived, after one message-time.
3. The last note has to wait for all ten messages, so it starts nine message-times after the first: nine lots of 0.96 ms, about 8.6 ms.
4. Predict the effect: the chord is heard as a fast ripple rather than a single attack, which can be audible on tight material.

Running status shortens the spread by dropping repeated status bytes. USB MIDI 1.0 can carry many event packets per millisecond, so the same chord is usually much less spread there, although the exact timing depends on the device, the host and its driver.
